items.title: US Department of Labor secures court order requiring New Jersey employer to pay $700K in back wages, damages to 48 workers denied overtime pay
items.content_text: VOORHEES, NJ – The U.S. Department of Labor has obtained a consent judgment and final order in federal district court requiring a New Jersey drywall installer to pay $725,000 in back wages, damages, and civil money penalties after denying 48 workers overtime pay.The department’s Wage and Hour Division found that P & B Partitions Inc. failed to pay their employees for pre-shift work while they waited for transportation to their jobsites. The failure to pay constitutes a violation under the Fair Labor Standards Act’s overtime provisions.  “Tasks completed to prepare for the job, and in this case, while waiting to get to the worksite, is work that must be compensated,” said Wage and Hour Division District Director Charlene Rachor in Southern New Jersey. “Failing to pay workers overtime wages deprives them of their rights, and we will hold employers accountable for such actions.”The consent judgment requires P & B Partitions Inc. to pay $350,000 in back wages, an equal amount in liquidated damages to 48 workers, and requires payment of an additional $25,000 in civil penalties. The judgment was entered in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey on June 26, 2026.“The U.S. Department of Labor will pursue legal action to ensure that all employees receive the compensation they are legally owed,” said Regional Solicitor of Labor Jeffrey S. Rogoff in New York. “This case demonstrates that employers can face costly consequences if they do not comply with federal wage law.”Employees and employers can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). items.title: Consent judgment orders California-based home appliance company to pay $800K to 339 employees denied overtime pay
items.content_text: LOS ANGELES – The U.S. Department of Labor has obtained a consent judgment requiring a home appliance company to pay $800,000 in back wages and damages to 339 employees after an investigation found the company violated federal wage laws.The judgment comes after the department’s Wage and Hour Division investigated Coway USA Inc. and found that the employer paid employees on a piece-rate basis and failed to pay employees for time spent attending mandatory meetings, picking up and loading supplies, and performing work before and after their shifts, in violation of the Fair Labor Standards Act. Investigators also found that Coway did not include nondiscretionary incentives, bonuses, and commissions in overtime pay calculations and frequently reduced the number of hours employees recorded working on their timecards.Entered in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California on Sept. 9, the consent judgment requires Coway to record all hours the implicated employees worked, including time they spend picking up supplies, attending mandatory training, and communicating with customers before and after appointments. Coway is also required to give employees pay statements that show their hours worked, services provided to customers, and the rate Coway paid for the hours and services. The consent judgment orders Coway USA Inc. to pay $400,000 in unpaid overtime wages and an equal amount in damages to 339 employees working in the greater metro areas of Los Angeles, New York City, and Washington, D.C. The company also agreed to pay $10,000 in penalties for willful violations. Coway USA Inc. is a subsidiary of Coway Co. Ltd., a multinational company specializing in home appliances. The company installs and maintains various appliances, including water and air filtration products throughout the U.S.Employers and employees can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). items.title: US Department of Labor announces field assistance bulletin withdrawing 3 opinion letters on tipped employees
items.content_text: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division today announced the issuance of a new field assistance bulletin addressing the treatment of related duties performed by tipped employees under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Field Assistance Bulletin No. 2026-1 brings the division’s guidance on tipped employees with dual jobs into alignment with current regulations.The bulletin withdraws the division’s 1979, 1980, and 1985 opinion letters concerning the application of dual jobs regulations to tipped employees. The withdrawal of the three opinion letters is necessary because they no longer reflect the division’s policy or interpretation of the FLSA. The bulletin also clarifies that the current dual jobs regulation focuses on whether an employee performs duties related to the employee’s tipped occupation, rather than imposing a specific percentage-based limit on the time an employee may spend performing related, non-tipped duties within that occupation.The publication of the new bulletin follows a 2024 federal court decision that vacated the department’s 2021 dual jobs final rule. After that decision, the department removed the regulatory text adopted under the 2021 rule and reinstated the original dual jobs regulations.The new field assistance bulletin clarifies that no current Wage and Hour Division guidance relies on the former percentage-based limit on the time a tipped employee may spend performing related, non-tipped duties, commonly known as the 80/20 rule.
